analysis.one_liner: Bans lawsuits blaming food companies and sellers for obesity and weight-related health problems.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 53 cosponsors from both parties, never received a hearing or vote in the House Judiciary Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have barred any new federal or state lawsuit against food manufacturers, marketers, distributors, advertisers, sellers, and their trade associations claiming that eating their products caused weight gain, obesity, or related health conditions. It would have also immediately dismissed any such lawsuits already in court. Narrow exceptions remained for broken express warranties, knowingly illegal marketing or labeling that someone relied on, and enforcement actions by the FTC or FDA [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Food and beverage companies, restaurants, advertisers, distributors, and trade associations would gain immunity from a category of civil lawsuits, avoiding litigation costs and damage awards over obesity-related claims [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits bringing any new civil action in federal or state court against a food manufacturer, marketer, distributor, advertiser, seller, or trade association for injuries tied to a person's accumulated eating, weight gain, obesity, or associated health conditions [S2] [S3].
Requires courts to immediately dismiss any such lawsuits already pending on the date of enactment, and freezes discovery (the evidence-gathering stage) while a motion to dismiss is decided [S3].

Keeps three narrow escape hatches: breaches of express contract or warranty unrelated to weight, claims of knowing violations of food marketing or labeling statutes that a person justifiably relied on, and enforcement by the FTC or FDA [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: People harmed by foods or by misleading food marketing would lose the ability to sue in most obesity-related cases, and state courts would lose the power to hear these claims; juries and state legislatures deciding liability rules would be overridden by federal law [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill strips consumers of their day in court for an entire category of injury claims, including pending cases, and preempts state tort law — the traditional way individuals hold companies accountable for harmful products [S3].

The exceptions are narrow and hard to meet: a consumer would have to prove a company knowingly broke a specific labeling or marketing statute, that the consumer justifiably relied on that violation, and that this reliance was the direct cause of the injury [S3].

The bill's stated premise is that weight gain and obesity 'cannot be attributed to the consumption of any specific food or beverage,' a legislative finding that would effectively settle a contested scientific and legal question in the industry's favor before any court could weigh the evidence [S3].

Supporters' good-faith case: lawsuits blaming a single food or seller for obesity are legally weak, costly to defend, and at odds with the idea of personal responsibility, and health policy is better set by legislatures and regulators than by courts [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters argued the bill stopped frivolous lawsuits and kept food policy in legislatures and regulators rather than courtrooms [S3]. But the shield is sweeping: it covers every seller, marketer, and trade association, dismisses pending cases outright, and leaves consumers only narrow, hard-to-prove exceptions. The main practical effect is to eliminate legal accountability for obesity-related claims without creating any substitute protection for the people those claims were meant to serve.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, sent to a subcommittee in June 2007, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Dan Boren introduced the bill on May 7, 2007, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1] [S5].
On June 4, 2007, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law — the last action ever taken on the bill [S5].
No hearing, committee vote, or House floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers kept the ability to sue food companies over obesity-related claims, and state courts kept jurisdiction over them; the food industry did not get the litigation shield it sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers who kept their right to sue

for.what_they_did: Backed 'commonsense consumption' laws shielding food sellers from obesity lawsuits, a campaign this bill echoed

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat introduced the bill and 9 Democrats joined 44 Republicans as cosponsors, but the Democratic-controlled Judiciary Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would bar consumers from suing them over weight- and obesity-related injuries, dismissing pending cases outright. That immunity comes directly out of consumers' legal recourse, with only narrow exceptions left standing [S2] [S3].

industries.industry: Restaurants, fast-food chains, and food retailers
industries.note: As sellers and marketers of 'qualified products,' they would be shielded from suits by customers claiming harm from their products — the classic target of obesity litigation [S3].
The bill explicitly covers advertisers and industry trade groups, extending the liability shield beyond manufacturers to everyone in the marketing chain [S3].
